Company framing: a 'flexible land acquisition strategy' of buying or optioning finished lots or buying raw land for development, with land banking used 'on a limited and strategic basis' (FY2025 10-K); the CEO calls the position 'predominantly self-developed, on-balance-sheet' (Q3 2026 release). No stated owned/optioned target or years-of-supply target. Raw land takes two to four years to become an active community. Direction of travel: owned lots have fallen six straight quarters from a peak of 61,893 (Q2 2022) while controlled lots rose 18.1% in Q3 2026 as management pursued finished-lot takedowns from developers and smaller projects.
Financing summary: LGI Homes is one of the most land-heavy public builders: at September 30, 2026 it owned 50,270 of its 58,400 lots (86%) and controlled only 8,130 (14%) through ordinary purchase and option contracts, and its CEO describes the position as predominantly self-developed and on balance sheet. It funds land with a roughly $1.17 billion bank revolver agented by Wells Fargo (borrowing base tied to land, lots and homes; $411.2 million drawn at quarter-end) plus $1.1 billion of senior notes due 2028, 2029 and 2032, and a $50 million non-recourse loan against its rental homes. Its only disclosed land-banking program, with one unnamed third-party land banker, ran from 2022 and was fully repurchased by June 30, 2026, so LGI currently has no land banker. Net debt to capital is 40.6%, high for the group, the lot supply is about 12 years at the 2026 closing pace, two thirds of owned lots are still raw or under development, and the credit agreement blocks buybacks and dividends through December 31, 2026: that combination (heavy owned land, elevated leverage, nothing due in 2026 or 2027 but $400 million of 8.75% notes due December 2028, and management saying it now sees more finished-lot takedown opportunities) is the opening for a land banker.
Lots note: Owned 50,270 = 34,119 raw/under development + 16,151 finished (the finished count includes 2,147 completed homes and information centers and 1,626 homes in progress; about 12,378 vacant finished lots per the earnings call). 'Optioned' is the company's 'controlled' figure. years_supply is computed, not company-stated: 58,400 lots divided by the 4,700 midpoint of 2026 closings guidance (4,600 to 4,800). The Q3 2026 10-Q Note 10 separately shows 8,622 lots under land option and purchase contracts ($390.6M aggregate purchase price, $17.9M deposits); the 492-lot difference from 8,130 is not reconciled in the filing. Trend: 70,899 lots at 12/31/2024, 60,842 at 12/31/2025 (51,890 owned / 8,952 controlled), 59,028 at 3/31/2026, 57,406 at 6/30/2026. Segment split at 12/31/2025 (owned/controlled): Central 19,108/517; Southeast 13,372/2,629; Northwest 5,877/1,250; West 8,367/3,323; Florida 5,166/1,233 (FY2025 10-K). The 9/30/2026 segment split was not retrievable.

It also sold non-strategic land (more than $100M expected in FY2026, per the CEO) and did a model-home sale-leaseback. Financing summary: Beazer Homes is no longer a stand-alone borrower: Dream Finders Homes bought it for $33.50 a share in cash (about $878.4M of equity) on 2026-10-20, and Beazer's land and debt now sit inside Dream Finders' land-light, option-heavy model. For a competing land banker, Beazer's remaining owned land and any future land-bank work are now Dream Finders decisions, and Millrose is already in both the land and the capital structure.

At closing about 7,000 of the owned homesites moved to Millrose under options to Dream Finders, so the owned share is now far lower.

Land strategy: Finished-lot buyer in third-party master-planned communities, plus selective self-development. Company framing: 'We rely on strong developer partnerships' (Chris Little, President of Central Texas and Florida, July 2026) and growth 'driven by ... partnering with best-in-class developers' (April 2026 release). The exceptions are Juniper Springs in Lockhart, TX, where Perry is itself the developer of about 1,400 homesites, and new acreage-lot product in Central Texas and Dallas-Fort Worth. Metrics source: Middleburg platform infrastructure page
Land strategy: Capital-light site control rather than land ownership: the land team sources off-market sites directly (750+ scored and 30+ contracted a year across eight states and 30+ metros), holds them under contract through entitlement, and closes the land when construction financing is in place. No stated owned/optioned target because it does not operate a lot pipeline. Company figures: 52 projects and 18,000+ units under control and in development, about 20 projects and 5,600 units under construction, 18 to 20 starts planned for 2026.
Financing summary: NOT A FOR-SALE HOMEBUILDER: Middleburg develops, builds and operates rental housing (apartments and Hamlet single-family build-to-rent), so it does not buy finished lots on a takedown schedule and is at best an edge-case land-banking customer. It funds each project separately: institutional joint-venture equity (Harbor Group International is the one LP named in 2026), its own GP co-invest from a discretionary fund series (GP Fund III closed at $125M in February 2026), bank construction loans (Truist and US Bank named) and agency take-out debt (Freddie Mac via Newmark). Sites are held under contract while GP fund money carries them through zoning and entitlement, and land usually closes together with the construction loan, which removes most of the need for a third-party land banker. The room for one is narrow: pre-development land carry or horizontal development on BTR sites if its 52-project, 18,000-unit pipeline outruns GP fund capital, especially in the new Western markets. The firm is also a capital provider (preferred equity and mezzanine funds for other sponsors), and its finance bench turned over in 2026, so relationships there are in flux. Corporate debt, cash and leverage are not public.

Its 2025-2026 US land releases describe outright closings, either raw land or finished lots bought from master developers, and none mentions a land banker or option partner. That makes Mattamy an under-penetrated prospect for land banking, not an existing land-bank user. Owned-versus-optioned lot data is not public: financial statements go only to certified noteholders through Intralinks.

Land strategy: HFHI owns no homebuilding land (land, buildings and equipment were $5.0M net at June 30, 2026). Each independent affiliate sources and holds its own land. HFHI supports them with acquisition, predevelopment and construction loans from Habitat Capital and the US Property Acquisition Fund, plus grants; there is no stated owned/optioned target and no lot-option structure.
Financing summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder: Habitat for Humanity International (HFHI) is a nonprofit whose independent local affiliates buy land, build and sell the homes; HFHI itself holds no homebuilding land and has no lot-option programme. It is not a plausible land-banking customer in the conventional sense: there is no central land buyer or takedown pipeline, homes are sold at affordable prices to lower-income buyers, and land capital is philanthropic or concessionary. HFHI funds affiliates' land through its wholly owned CDFI, Habitat Capital ($46.8M lent to 31 affiliates in FY2026), and the US Property Acquisition Fund, an $82.5M vehicle launched March 2025 that borrows at 2% to 6.01% from JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Enterprise Community Loan Fund and foundations and on-lends to affiliates for land and property purchases. Consolidated borrowings were about $110M at June 30, 2026 ($57.1M notes payable, $52.9M investor notes backed by affiliate notes), against $767M of total assets. Any opening for a land banker would be one-off deals with individual large affiliates, or learning from the Property Acquisition Fund structure, not a corporate relationship with HFHI.

The same land pipeline feeds the build-to-rent affiliate SimplyHome (more than 10,800 rental homes built), and the only named lender anywhere in the group is Churchill Real Estate, which provided SimplyHome a $255 million bridge facility arranged by JLL in 2023. No land banker, lot-option financier or outside equity partner has been named publicly. It is a plausible land-banking customer rather than a current one: the land sits on a family balance sheet, the 1,457 closings in the 2026 Builder 100 are well under half the 3,351 closings/units the company cited for 2022, and since August 2025 the group has been run by a finance and capital-markets CEO (ex-Highland Homes, ex-TPG Capital) with a new CFO (April 2026), a Chief Investment Officer and a newly promoted land president whose remit includes 'strategic partnerships'.

For a land banker this is a plausible but parent-gated customer: Edge runs its own acquisition and entitlement team and buys land outright on entitlement-contingent contracts, while the parent has both a stated push toward optioned lots and leverage that rose sharply with the Tri Pointe deal (net D/E about 1.4x at September 2026).

Land strategy: Not framed publicly as land-light or land-heavy, and no owned-versus-optioned target is stated. Evidence suggests it buys and develops most of its own land in secondary and rural Northwest markets (regional land acquisition, forward planning and land development teams; direct land purchases from owners), supplemented by buying finished or pipeline lots from other builders and developers and by city partnerships that bring land inside urban growth boundaries in exchange for affordability commitments.

No land banker, lot-option financier or institutional capital partner is named anywhere, and no public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. One unconfirmed lead: a search-result summary of a Builder article lists Hayden Homes among strategic builder investors in Avila Real Estate Capital's first homebuilder debt fund (closed July 2025).

Land strategy: Mixed and not quantified. Challenger Homes sells in about 11 Colorado communities, several inside third-party master plans (Sterling Ranch, Wolf Ranch, Meridian Ranch); whether those lots are bought finished, optioned or self-developed is not disclosed. In February 2024 the controlling owner bought back Green Brick Partners' minority stake for about $64 million, removing its one institutional equity partner. No land banker or lot-option partner is named anywhere; National Builder Group buys only finished lots a few at a time, so the room for a land banker is mainly Challenger Homes' Colorado community pipeline and any larger finished-lot takedowns the owner-operators cannot stage, where land-bank pricing would compete with roughly 10% affiliate money that carries a parent guarantee.

Known land bankers: Kennedy Lewis, Developers Capital Fund, GSH Land Fund, unnamed land banker(s)
Credit ratings: None found (no rated public bonds; debt was bank revolver and private term loan)
Metrics source: UHG FY2025 earnings release (8-K Ex. 99.1, filed 2026-03-12)
Land strategy: Land-light, in the company's own words: it buys finished lots through lot option contracts with third-party developers, related-party developers and land bank partners, putting up deposits of typically 15-20% of the purchase price with staggered takedowns. On land bank contracts UHG usually pays development costs and is reimbursed the next month. At 2025-12-31, 96% of about 7,200 owned or controlled lots were controlled through options. In 2023 CEO Jack Micenko said UHG would not carry large owned lot inventories and would hold lots as options through Pennington, the Nieri-affiliated land business. No numeric target was stated. Financing summary: Until May 2026 United Homes Group (Great Southern Homes, Rosewood Communities; Columbia, SC) was a Nasdaq-listed, almost fully land-light builder: at 2025 year end it owned 284 lots and controlled 6,941 through lot option contracts (96%), with $40.5M of deposits against $270.6M of remaining option purchase price. Lots came from third-party developers, land developers affiliated with controlling holder Michael Nieri (Land to Lots, PC Land Development, Pennington Development) and land bank partners, including a $150M land fund agreed with Developers Capital Fund LLC in 2024 and a 'third party land bank' called GSH Land Fund, LLC. Corporate funding was a $220M Wells Fargo-agented secured construction revolver ($78.2M drawn) and a $70M subordinated term loan agented by Kennedy Lewis (SOFR + 675-775 bps); both needed covenant relief in Sept 2025 and March 2026 and were repaid and terminated when Stanley Martin (Daiwa House) closed its all-cash merger on 2026-05-04. UHG is now a wholly owned Stanley Martin subsidiary, so new land-bank capital would be decided and priced at the Stanley Martin/Daiwa level. Those parents have far more balance sheet than UHG had, which may reduce the need for outside land-bank capital in the South Carolina markets.

This is the last public lot count: no Q1 2026 10-Q was filed before the merger closed, and the company deregistered (Form 15, 2026-05-14).

Land strategy: Mixed, leaning owner-developer. In Richmond it assembles and entitles tracts itself and develops master-planned communities (Edgebrook: 45 acres, 387 townhomes; The Aire: about 2,200 homes; River Mill: about 1,000 homes) in which HHHunt Homes builds. Elsewhere the land team buys finished lots for homebuilding and sites for apartments. The company tells land sellers it is privately held, diversified and long-term, and that it is actively looking for land in the Southeast. No stated owned-versus-optioned target.
Financing summary: HHHunt is a private, family-owned, diversified residential company, not a pure for-sale homebuilder: it builds homes in Virginia and North Carolina (580 closed in 2025 per its own site), develops its own master-planned communities around Richmond through HHHunt Communities, and owns and manages about 8,885 apartments in 27 communities that it describes as income-producing ballast. Nothing public shows a land banker, lot-option financier or outside equity partner on the for-sale side; lots come from its own land-development arm and from finished-lot purchases negotiated by a four-person land acquisition team. The only named financing in public sources is property-level apartment debt (HUD-insured construction loans arranged by Berkadia, and a 2022 ACRE debt-fund acquisition loan). Corporate credit facilities, homebuilding lot lines and balance-sheet figures are not disclosed. It is a plausible but small land-banking customer: the opening is finished-lot or takedown structures for HHHunt Homes in Raleigh and Wilmington, where it has no in-house master-plan pipeline, and the finance relationship passes from Ann Kelly to Steve Brant on 2027-07-01.

Known land bankers: TPG Angelo Gordon (Reported)
Land strategy: Mixed and shifting land-lighter. In 2020 the company was described as self-developing most of its lots (buying raw land, entitling it and installing infrastructure), for example the 400-lot Orchard Park subdivision in Centerton. Since late 2025 it has added finished-lot option agreements with Essential Housing and a developer partnership with Calara, while still buying raw land outright (62.85 acres in Gravette, Oct 2026). No stated owned/optioned target.
Financing summary: Private, 100% ESOP-owned builder with no public debt, ratings or financial statements, so almost all of its capital structure is not publicly disclosed. What county records (as reported by Talk Business) show is a three-part land model in Northwest Arkansas: land banking of finished lots with TPG Angelo Gordon's Essential Housing (three recorded two-year option deals from Dec 2025 to Oct 2026 covering 248 lots and about $22.2M), finished lots bought or contracted from third-party developers (Calara, Kinney Creek, Three Pistols, Saddle Hill Estates), and raw land or lot purchases funded with short local bank loans (First National Bank of Fort Smith, North American Savings Bank, earlier City Bank of Lubbock). It also moves small batches of completed homes into a wholly owned rental affiliate, Steppingstone Home Rentals LLC, financed by Arvest Bank. A competitor is already the incumbent land banker, but only Northwest Arkansas deals are visible; Springfield, Joplin and the new Tulsa market show no public land-bank activity, which is where room for a second provider is most plausible.

Metrics source: Business Observer: Builder plans 825-home community in south Sarasota County
Land strategy: Owns and develops most of its own land, by choice. Company wording: 'we purchase the land we develop, build and sell the homes'. Founder's framing (November 2025): 'I'm a land guy', holding cash to buy land, will 'go more in the land business', and notes that the stock market penalises public builders for holding land. It also builds inside third-party master plans (Lakewood Ranch, Wellen Park, Kingston by Cameratta Companies) and in North River Ranch, developed by the family affiliate Neal Land & Neighborhoods. No stated owned/optioned target.
Financing summary: Neal Communities is a conventional for-sale homebuilder, privately owned by founder Pat Neal, and it publishes no financial statements, lot counts, lenders or facilities. What is public points to a self-funded, land-heavy model: the company says it purchases the land it develops, a 2024 Business Observer profile credits it with an aversion to debt, and in November 2025 Pat Neal said he is holding cash to buy land and expects to go further into the land business as other builders give up positions. Infrastructure is financed where possible through special district (CDD / stewardship district) municipal bonds, which he has said cost less than bank development loans, and raw land is typically tied up under long contracts with the sellers and closed only once permits are in hand (the $34.1M, 788-acre Alva purchase closed in August 2026 after about four years). No land banker, lot-option financier or outside capital partner is named anywhere public. As a land-banking customer it is plausible but not an obvious one: the owner prefers to own land and has cash, yet 2025 revenue fell about 27% to roughly $586M, he rated 2025 margins 3 out of 10, a new president arrived around August 2026, and large new positions (Alva, Boca Royale at Wellen Park, Kingston, Burnt Store Road) all need development capital.

Credit ratings: None (no rated debt). The two affiliated capital corporations are rated by Aeris, per the budget justification.
Metrics source: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer: Neighborhood Reinvestment Corp (Form 990 data for fiscal year ending September 2025)
Land strategy: None of its own. NeighborWorks America owns no development land and controls no lots; each member nonprofit sources its own sites (often donated, public or infill parcels, or community land trust land) with grant money, local subsidy and loans from the two affiliated capital corporations. The company's own framing is an 'intermediary' that supplies flexible, early-stage 'risk capital' grants that members can use for acquisition, predevelopment and development.
Financing summary: NOT a conventional for-sale homebuilder, and not a plausible land-banking customer. NeighborWorks America is a federally chartered nonprofit funded almost entirely by an annual congressional appropriation ($158 million core in fiscal 2025; total revenue $179 million; total assets only $68 million). It does not buy land, hold lots, borrow to build or sell homes: it passes grants to 248 independent local nonprofits, and those members built and sold the homes counted in the Builder 100 (875 closings in 2025). Land and construction money for the members comes from grants, local subsidy and two affiliated nonprofit lenders, Community Housing Capital and NeighborWorks Capital, which lend only or mainly to the network (land acquisition, predevelopment, construction; $169 million lent in fiscal 2024). The room for a commercial land banker is close to nil at the national level; at most a few of the largest member nonprofits could be one-off lot-option counterparties, and they would compare the price with subsidised nonprofit loans. Funding risk is real: the President's fiscal 2026 budget proposed ending the appropriation.

Land strategy: Not stated by the company. Trade press describes growth through its own land acquisition plus franchise-style brand partnerships (the company still advertises a Local Builder franchise programme asking partners for $200,000 to $1,000,000 of capital). In practice it sells in a mix of its own neighbourhoods and lots inside other developers' master-planned communities, including its parent's Verdancia. No owned-versus-optioned split or target is public.
Financing summary: View Homes is a conventional for-sale, entry-level homebuilder and a plausible land-banking customer, but since early October 2025 it has been a subsidiary of Hunt Companies, a private, family-owned El Paso holding company, so its capital now comes through the parent and none of its own debt, lenders or lot counts are public. HousingWire framed the sale as a private builder squeezed by tight acquisition, development and construction lending pairing with patient capital, and expects Hunt to fund growth in existing markets. The parent also owns a lot source: Hunt Communities develops master-planned communities in El Paso and Austin (about 10,000 acres and more than 15,000 single-family lots over their life), and View Homes is one of the builders in Hunt's Verdancia in Horizon City. Outside El Paso (Colorado Springs, Denver, Northern Colorado, Las Cruces, San Antonio, New Braunfels) Hunt has no communities of its own on its site, so View Homes still has to source lots from third parties there; that is where a land banker has room, with the decision likely sitting with the CEO, the CFO and the Hunt-appointed board. No land banker, lot-option partner or lender to View Homes was named in any source opened.

Metrics source: Builder firm page (closings 943 in 2023, 912 in 2024; revenue $369M and $357M)
Land strategy: Mixed, leaning owned: the company says it knows 'where to acquire the best land' and develops in-house through Woodmere Development (own planned communities such as Morton Creek Ranch and a 270-acre project inside Beacon Hill), plus lots bought in others' master plans. No stated owned/optioned target.
Financing summary: Long Lake is a privately held, single-market Houston builder whose financing is not public: no SEC filings, rated debt, or announced credit facilities. It controls land through an affiliated developer, Woodmere Development Co., Ltd., under the same general-partner manager (Roger B. Medors), which bought a 494-acre tract near Bridgeland in Katy (2022) and 95 acres near Tomball in Montgomery County (closed October 2024, undisclosed price). It also builds in third-party master plans (Beacon Hill, Sunterra Lakes). No land banker, lot-option partner or capital partner is publicly named. Falling closings (943 in 2023 to 782 in 2025) and large owned raw-land tracts make it a plausible prospect for land-banking or lot-option capital, but there is no public sign it uses any.

Metrics source: No financial statements are public; the parent's About page gives only headline figures ($3.5B+ assets under management, 25K+ paper lots)
Land strategy: Vertically integrated rather than land-light: the company's own framing is that First America Homes 'leverages in-house land development' from The Signorelli Company's integrated platform. In practice it is mixed: parent-developed lots in Houston-area master plans, plus finished-lot purchases from third-party developers in Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and San Antonio. No owned-versus-optioned target is stated. The parent's land arm is also a lot seller: its 6,400-acre Austin Point lists nine outside builders and not First America Homes.
Financing summary: First America Homes is a conventional for-sale builder, but it is a division of a private developer rather than a stand-alone company, and nothing about its debt, lenders or balance sheet is public. Its land comes two ways: lots developed by the parent's own Land division (for example 359 lots at Azalea District in Valley Ranch, where it is the exclusive builder), and finished homesites bought in other developers' communities in the 2026 expansion markets (81 lots at Leonard Trails in Anna, three Austin-area communities, nine San Antonio-area communities). The parent describes itself as well capitalized, cites $3.5B+ of assets under management and 25,000+ paper lots, and says it is buying positions from industry partners that want to shrink. No land banker, lot-option financier or lender is named anywhere public. It is a plausible land-banking customer, most likely at the parent level (funding the parent's lot development pipeline or the builder's fast growth toward a stated 5,000 homes a year by 2035), and the people to approach are the parent's CFO and Land division.

Metrics source: McBride Homes: History page
Land strategy: Owns and develops its own land, in the company's framing a selective, margin-first approach. The CEO told Builder (Sept 2026, as relayed by STL.News) that McBride matches starts to demand, can cut starts because it is private, and follows a 'Next Exit' strategy of exurban sites near interstates chosen on job growth, access and land cost, with plans to grow beyond current volume over five to ten years. Land is sometimes bought through project-level entities (a 31.8-acre Union, MO purchase in Dec 2022 was made by St. Andrews Drive Development LLC, per the broker's release). No owned-versus-optioned target is stated.
Financing summary: Private company with no SEC filings or rated debt, so lenders, facility terms, debt and lot counts are not public. What is visible is a self-development model: an in-house land arm (McBride Land Strategy) buys, entitles and develops large master plans, topped up with finished lots bought from other builders, builder joint ventures and public-private structures in which a city or county carries land or infrastructure cost. No land banker, lot-option financier or outside capital partner is named in any source opened, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. The pipeline announced since 2025 is large relative to roughly 750 to 800 closings a year (854 lots at Havenwood, 700+ at the Jamestown Mall site, 587 in Rolla), which makes McBride a plausible land-banking prospect on paper, but there is no public sign that it uses third-party land capital today.

Metrics source: Century Communities Q3 2026 results press release (8-K Exhibit 99.1). HistoryMaker has no stand-alone figures; parent metrics are on the century-communities record.
Land strategy: Before the sale: an integrated family platform, with Jabez Development (land acquisition, entitlement and development) feeding HistoryMaker Homes (for-sale) and ONM Living (build-to-rent); no owned/optioned split or target was ever published. After the sale: Century's strategy applies. Century describes its lots as 54.9% owned and 45.1% controlled at 2026-09-30, says it is moving toward lower-deposit lot contracts, and will take finished lots in DFW from Jabez Development on current and future communities.
Financing summary: Conventional for-sale builder that no longer finances itself: since 2026-10-07 its communities, lots and work in process sit on Century Communities' balance sheet, bought for about $160.2M of initial cash that Century drew on its $1.2B unsecured revolver (U.S. Bank agent, upsized and extended to November 2030 one week earlier). HistoryMaker's own pre-sale bank lines, lot counts and any land-bank arrangements were never public. The family model was integrated: sister company Jabez Development developed lots and HistoryMaker built on them; Jabez was not sold and keeps developing and delivering lots to Century under an ongoing contract, so the seller is now Century's lot developer in Dallas-Fort Worth. Century says it uses land banking only on a very limited basis and controls 45.1% of its 60,969 lots (2026-09-30, before HistoryMaker) through options, while its revolver balance rose from $51.5M to $456.0M in nine months and its stated priority is to hold debt to capital. Room for a land banker therefore sits in two places: Century's enlarged DFW lot pipeline (a parent-level conversation), and Jabez Development, a private developer that now carries horizontal risk for a public builder and has no disclosed capital partner.

Land strategy: Owns and develops most of its land through the parent. Rhodes Enterprises describes itself as vertically integrated: it master-plans and develops communities and Esperanza Homes builds in them. Stated holdings: Tres Lagos, McAllen (2,567 acres, 30-year plan, active); Bentsen Palm, Mission (2,600 acres, active since 2004); La Sienna, Edinburg (726 acres, 'now part of the Rhodes portfolio', about 350 acres undeveloped); Mirabella, Corpus Christi (about 300 acres, over 1,150 homes, active development); Estrella, Brownsville (proposed, over 3,200 homes). The family originally bought about 10,000 acres of Hidalgo County farmland. Outside the master plans it builds smaller stand-alone communities (Weslaco, San Juan, Mercedes, Harlingen, Brownsville, Laredo); whether those lots are self-developed or bought finished is not stated, and no owned-versus-optioned split is published.
Financing summary: Esperanza Homes is the building arm of family-owned Rhodes Enterprises, which develops its own master-planned land and hands lots to its builder, so land is financed inside the family group rather than through options or a land banker. No land-bank, lot-option or outside equity partner is named in any source opened. Public records, as compiled by an aggregator, show the group borrowing from regional banks (International Bank of Commerce, Third Coast Bank, Bank OZK) through per-market Esperanza LLCs and development LLCs, including a $75M Third Coast Bank deed of trust recorded in late 2026. Tres Lagos infrastructure is partly reimbursed through a City of McAllen TIRZ and a public improvement district. It is a plausible but unproven land-banking customer: the growth plan (1,000 closings by 2027, new Laredo and Corpus Christi divisions, a 3,200-home Brownsville master plan) needs capital beyond the legacy family land, yet the group has so far chosen bank debt and self-development.

Land strategy: Capital-light by design. JCCG finds, entitles and develops sites and builds the homes, but under general-contractor or fee-build agreements for the investor or developer that owns the project; where JCCG originates the deal, the capital partner closes on the land with it. The company does not describe owned or optioned lot positions and states no land-light target.
Financing summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder: JCCG is a private, founder-owned build-to-rent general contractor and lot developer, so most of the land and construction capital in its projects belongs to its clients, not to JCCG. Named or described capital sources are an unnamed publicly traded REIT (five communities), an unnamed publicly traded investment firm (which closed on the Dawsonville land together with JCCG in November 2024), a Trinitas Ventures / PCCP joint venture, NexMetro, AREY Group, BLDG Real Estate and a Scottsdale family office. Earlier (2021 to 2023) JCCG developed communities and sold them whole to institutional owners, including four communities of 971 homes closed in 2023. JCCG's own lenders, credit lines and balance sheet are not publicly disclosed, and no land banker or lot-option financier is named anywhere in its releases. For a land banker it is a weak direct customer (no for-sale takedown schedule, lots end up in rental ownership) but a possible channel: it delivered 1,040 finished lots in 2025, has a four-person land team, and its investor clients could use lot or development funding between land closing and vertical start.

Land strategy: Not publicly stated. Public records point to owning lots and land through the operating LLCs and the affiliated JNC Development, Inc., financed with bank debt; the company says it develops its own subdivisions ('we work to develop subdivisions, parks, and communities') and also buys into third-party master plans (e.g. Lakeside at Tessera on Lake Travis, Austin).
Financing summary: Saratoga Homes is a private, family-owned Texas builder with no public debt, no SEC filings and no published lot counts. Recorded county deeds of trust (via a data aggregator) show it funds construction and lots with secured bank loans from Texas and regional banks (International Bank of Commerce, Texas Capital Bank, Flagstar, WestStar, Citizens Bank of Las Cruces), largely house-by-house or project loans in the operating LLCs and its affiliated JNC Development, Inc. No land banker, lot-option partner, capital partner or JV is publicly named, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. For a land banker this is open ground: a bank-financed family builder of about 700 closings a year that appears to own its land and lots through family entities.

Credit ratings: None (no rated debt)
Metrics source: Kentucky SOS entity record (private LLC; no financials published)
Land strategy: Owns and develops most of its land, in the company's own words developing its own neighborhoods (Chilesburg, Willow Bend, Masterson Station/Greendale named in its brochure) and self-entitling subdivisions in Knox County, TN. No stated land-light or option target.
Financing summary: Ball Homes is a privately held, family-owned LLC with no public debt and no SEC filings, so its credit facilities, leverage and lot counts are not disclosed. Public records show it acting as its own land developer: it applies for its own zoning and subdivision approvals (e.g. an 87-lot, later 95-lot, Buttermilk Road subdivision in Knox County approved Feb-Mar 2026, a 50-lot West Gallaher Ferry subdivision approved June 2025, and the multi-phase Chilesburg master plan in Lexington). Its lending relationships appear to be with Kentucky community banks (Central Bank and Traditional Bank show up most often as mortgagees on its property records), and it runs an affiliated mortgage company (Walden Mortgage Group). No land banker, lot-option financier or outside equity partner is publicly linked to it, so a land banker would be pitching a builder that today owns and develops most of its land on bank credit.

Metrics source: Lombardo Homes: About Us
Land strategy: Owns and develops its own land, by its own description: operations span land acquisition, land development, lot sales to other builders and purchases of developed lots from other developers. No land-light target or owned-versus-optioned split is published. A local news item seen only in search results describes a Macomb Township rezoning petition for land it expects to start developing around 2028, which, if accurate, means it carries raw land for years through entitlement.
Financing summary: Lombardo Homes is a conventional for-sale homebuilder, privately owned by the Lombardo family, with no public debt and no public financial statements; no lender, credit facility, land banker, lot-option partner or outside investor is named in any source opened in this run. The company presents itself as a self-performing land developer: it buys and develops land, sells lots to other builders and also buys finished lots from other developers, which points to family equity and (undisclosed) bank debt carrying the land rather than a land-bank programme. The family also owns an apartment business and a custom-home brand run from the same Shelby Township office, so the group has assets beyond homebuilding. It is a plausible land-banking customer (roughly 700 closings a year across Southeast Michigan, St. Louis and Columbia, with raw land held through entitlement), but nothing public shows it has used one, and the decision would rest with the family owners.

Credit ratings: None (private, no rated debt)
Metrics source: On Top of the World Communities: About ('remains completely debt-free and privately owned'); colenbuilt.com home page also says 'debt-free company'
Land strategy: Owns most / all: develops its own land. The Colen family bought the 13,000-acre Circle Square Ranch in 1975 and has developed On Top of the World there since 1982; Calesa Township (launched 2020) covers about 1,500 acres with about 5,000 homes in 19 neighborhoods planned over 15 to 20 years. No stated optioned-lot target.
Financing summary: Not a conventional for-sale homebuilder and not a plausible land-banking customer today: Colen Built is the family-owned developer-builder of its own master plans (On Top of the World 55+, Calesa Township, Melody Preserve) on land the Colen family has owned since buying the 13,000-acre Circle Square Ranch in Ocala in 1975. The company says publicly and repeatedly that it is debt-free and privately owned, so it self-funds land development and construction; no lender, facility, land banker, lot-option or capital partner is named in any public source found. A 2025 Vice President of Finance posting mentions managing banking relationships and supporting debt structuring, which suggests some bank relationships or contemplated borrowing, but no terms are public. Room for a land banker is minimal in Ocala; the only angles are a future expansion off the family land or the family as a seller of land.

Metrics source: No balance-sheet data public (private, unrated). Indicative only: Elementix shows about $281M of cumulative recorded mortgage filings (530 filings, 2015 to 2026) across 132 Fleet-linked entities, which is not a debt balance
Land strategy: Owns and self-develops. The affiliate Lackland Holdings acquires residentially zoned land, develops it (often into one-acre-plus homesites in exurban DFW counties) and sells lots to Riverside and to other builders; Riverside's in-house counsel described taking lots down from the development side through scheduled lot takedowns. No stated owned/optioned target and no third-party land banker. Lackland says it is 'always open' to buying more residential land or finished single-family lots.
Financing summary: Riverside is the homebuilding arm of Tim Fleet's Lackland Holdings, which buys and develops land in-house and sells finished lots to Riverside and to other builders, so the group already acts as its own land bank. Lackland's website says plainly that it is not interested in new financing sources and that it uses its own equity plus bank financing when necessary; it also holds income properties it says it never sells. Public-record listings point to Texas and regional banks (Simmons Bank, Vista Bank, Clayton Bank and Trust, American National Bank & Trust, Pinnacle, Vantage Bank Texas) lending to Riverside and to single-purpose Lackland land entities; no facility terms, lot counts or balance-sheet figures are public. This is a conventional for-sale builder (about 650 closings a year, DFW only) but a low-probability land-banking customer on its own stated terms; the realistic openings are selling it lots or a deal-by-deal partnership, which Lackland's site invites, and both run through Tim Fleet.

Metrics source: Alabama Secretary of State business entity record: Stone Martin Builders, LLC
Land strategy: Appears to own and develop most of its land (inferred, not stated by the company). The company describes itself as building homes and developing its own communities, invites landowners to sell to it through a land-submissions page, and holds land in an affiliate (SMB Land, LLC) with bank liens. It has stated no land-light target and published no owned versus optioned split.
Financing summary: Stone Martin is a conventional for-sale homebuilder that funds itself privately: owner equity through a holding company (Sky Holdings, Inc.) and secured bank credit, with nothing rated, registered or disclosed. State lien records show its land affiliate, SMB Land, LLC, borrowing from Texas Capital Bank (since 2020, renewed in 2025) and from smaller regional lenders (Southern States Bank, BankPlus, Listerhill Credit Union), which points to a traditional buy-develop-and-own land model financed loan by loan. No land banker, lot-option partner, outside equity investor or joint-venture land partner is named in any public source opened, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. For a land banker that means an open field but a small one: roughly 650 to 800 closings a year across secondary Alabama markets, with a CEO who personally came up through land.

Land strategy: Owns and self-develops (not land-light): the company describes itself as a neighborhood developer, buys raw farmland and entitles and develops it in phases; no stated option target and no public mention of lot-option or land-bank structures. Job-board search snippets (pages since removed, not opened) show it advertising a Director of Land Acquisition for Greater Milwaukee, which suggests it is adding land-buying capacity there.
Financing summary: Veridian is a conventional for-sale homebuilder, privately held and family-owned inside Forgewell Building Group, with no SEC filings or rated or public debt found and no disclosed lender, facility, land banker, lot-option partner or joint venture. It is its own land developer: it buys raw land, entitles it and develops it in phases with an in-house land development team, releasing finished homesites to its own buyers a few dozen at a time. Its pipeline is concentrated in very large self-developed communities (Hill Valley 841 homesites, Reiland Grove 561, Midpoint Meadows about 250 lots, Arrowood 300), which ties up capital for years and makes it a plausible land-banking prospect on paper. Against that, nothing public shows it has ever used third-party lot capital, the founder is still chairman and principal owner, and the group is vertically integrated (trades, millwork, property management), so any approach would be to David Simon, Chris Ehlers and the finance head directly.

Metrics source: SEC EDGAR company search: no matching companies
Land strategy: Buys finished homesites in master-planned communities from outside developers; the company credits long-standing developer relationships and fast response to new opportunities for its growth (CEO Kevin Egan, Dec 2022). No owned-versus-optioned target is published. Also builds in Castle Hills, developed by affiliate Bright Realty.
Financing summary: Private, family- and employee-owned builder (Bright Industries family; ESOP since 2017) with no SEC filings and no public debt, so its credit lines, lenders and lot counts are not public. Its model is to buy developer-finished lots in third-party master-planned communities in DFW and on the Colorado Front Range (Hillwood, at Treeline, is the named developer partner), plus lots in the family's own Castle Hills (Bright Realty). There is no public land-banking or lot-option partner and no public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon. The parent's balance sheet (Bright Industries, a diversified real-estate and energy family company) is the most likely funding backstop, which may reduce the need for outside land capital; equally, a builder of about 600 closings a year that buys finished lots from developers on takedown schedules is a natural lot-option prospect. The one land decision-maker is Forrest Hartley.

Land strategy: Mixed, with no stated owned-versus-optioned target. In Oklahoma the family entitles and develops much of its own land through affiliates and an in-house land development department, then builds it out. In Houston the lot source (own development or third-party developers) is not disclosed.
Financing summary: Home Creations is a private, family-owned, conventional for-sale builder with no public debt, no SEC filings and no published lender, credit facility, land banker or capital partner. What is public points to a self-funded, owner-developer model in Oklahoma: land development is an in-house function, co-founder Jalal Farzaneh is reported as owner of Shaz Investments (a Norman land developer), and an engineering firm says Home Creations hired it to plan a 760-acre, roughly 2,000-unit community in Norman. In Houston, entered in 2022, its lot sources are not disclosed: the company names no developer for its Houston communities. A 2015 profile quoted a company executive saying the owners reinvest most earnings and that a shortage of developed lots was the main brake on growth. It is a plausible land-banking customer on two fronts (the large Norman tract and Houston lot supply), but there is no public sign that the family has used outside land capital.

Metrics source: Pro Builder, 'Under-40 Home Builders: Working the Market' (2014-07-17): no balance-sheet data is public; founder describes bank development loans and no partnerships
Land strategy: Owns and develops most of its own land (not land-light). The company history says the founder finds and develops land himself, and the owner's affiliate Premium Land, LLC is the applicant on plats for Taber communities; the careers page advertises in-house development staff (a Development Coordinator to assist with land and lot acquisitions, and a Development Superintendent). No stated owned-versus-optioned target.
Financing summary: Private and founder-owned, so no balance sheet, lender or facility is public. What is public points to a self-funded developer-builder: the owner's affiliate Premium Land, LLC buys raw land, entitles it and develops lots for Homes by Taber, and in a 2014 interview the founder said he funds development with bank loans, deliberately without partners, and had built up more lots than he needed. No land banker, lot-option investor, JV or outside capital partner has been named anywhere, and no link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. It is a plausible but small land-banking customer: about 630 closings a year, nine of 29 communities just opening or coming soon, a new push into Tulsa, and a land pipeline carried on the owner's own balance sheet. The pitch would be to an owner who has so far preferred bank debt and full control.

Metrics source: Builder magazine firm page: Chesapeake Homes (2026 Builder 100)
Land strategy: Family vertical integration: the affiliated developer Wakefield Development acquires and develops land, and Chesapeake Homes builds on the finished lots. Wakefield's community list overlaps with Chesapeake communities such as River Club, Bridgewater, Coastal Club of the Carolinas, Traditions at Carolina Forest, Highgate and Ashville Park. No owned-versus-optioned framing or target is published. A 2026 land-acquisition job posting lists options, JVs and takedown structures among the deal types it handles.
Financing summary: Chesapeake Homes is a conventional for-sale builder: a private subsidiary of the Sandler family's L.M. Sandler & Sons, Inc. (Builder 100 rank 90; 631 closings and about $308M revenue in 2025). It has no public debt or SEC filings. Land comes mostly through a sister company, Wakefield Development, also owned by L.M. Sandler & Sons, which buys, entitles and develops lots across VA, NC, SC, MD, DE and GA, and has worked on other projects as a silent or side-by-side partner. The parent says it relies on 'long-standing banking and equity partnerships' and in-house capital, but no lender, facility or land banker is named publicly. A March 2026 posting for a Mid-Atlantic Land Acquisition Executive mentions options, joint ventures, takedowns, capital deployment with finance, and presentations to investment committees. That points to a growing, more structured land program, which makes it a plausible but unproven land-banking prospect. The likely contacts are Wakefield's project-finance/land lead, Clark Hetzler, and the owner Steve Sandler.

Land strategy: Not stated publicly. Evidence points to a mixed model: the company is the applicant and developer on its own subdivisions (333-unit Ridgeline Park phases in Nibley, with an in-house Director of Land Development in 2022, and land-development job listings under 'VHD, LLC'), and it also builds on lots inside third-party master-planned communities (Desert Color in St. George). Owned versus optioned split: not disclosed.
Financing summary: Conventional for-sale builder and a plausible land-banking customer, but with a strategic owner: Misawa Homes Co., Ltd. of Japan bought 51% in June 2024 through Misawa Homes America, Inc., and the company says it operates in partnership with Misawa while scaling toward 2,000 annual starts (it closed 600 homes in 2025) and entering neighboring markets such as Idaho. No lot counts, lenders, credit facilities or land-banking arrangements are public. Public records show it entitling and developing its own communities (for example a 333-unit plat in Nibley) as well as building in third-party master plans such as Desert Color. A treasurer job listing seen only in a search snippet refers to external banking partners, which suggests bank debt alongside Misawa equity. The gap between 600 closings and a 2,000-start goal implies a much larger lot pipeline than today, which is the opening for a land banker; whether Misawa prefers to fund land on balance sheet is not known.

Land strategy: Mixed, leaning owner-developer. The company does not publish a land-light target. It self-develops large communities in Volusia and Flagler counties (Plantation Bay, Mosaic) and St. Johns County (the 572-acre Crossroads tract), shares land risk through a builder partnership with phased takedowns at Seven Pines, and takes finished lots from master developers such as The PARC Group (EverRange), Wellen Park, Sunbridge and IronCrest.
Financing summary: ICI Homes is a private, family-owned company with no public debt, no SEC filings and no rating, so its lenders, facilities and balance sheet are not public. What is public is how it controls land: it develops its own communities in its Daytona Beach home market through special-purpose subsidiaries, it co-develops the 1,600-home Seven Pines community in Jacksonville in a partnership with David Weekley Homes that buys the land from the selling family in phases, and elsewhere it buys finished lots as a preferred builder from third-party master developers. No land banker, lot-option financier or outside capital partner is named in any source found, and there is no public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon. It is a conventional for-sale builder and a plausible land-banking prospect on paper (it carries developer-scale land and a 2025 trade feature says it will add land to the south and on the Gulf coast), but the owner stresses long-horizon private ownership, so appetite for off-balance-sheet structures is untested.

Metrics source: Strategy shift pays off for locally based homebuilder (Business Observer, 2023-05-19)
Land strategy: Asset-light by design rather than by option: the CEO has said the company enters markets where there is a single ('spot') lot opportunity because it carries much less risk, and the company's current land-acquisition job posting describes sourcing scattered, spot and infill lots from the MLS. It also solicits land sellers directly ('one or one-thousand lots') and takes finished homesites from master developers (West Port, Babcock Ranch, Brightshore). No owned/optioned split or stated target is published.
Financing summary: Private, founder-led and self-described 'builder-owned' Florida builder (554 to 555 closings in 2025) with no public debt, no SEC filings and no disclosed lender, credit facility, land banker or outside capital partner. It is a conventional for-sale builder, but its land model is unusual: most homes go up one at a time on scattered infill lots it buys from individual owners and the MLS in pre-platted communities (Cape Coral, Lehigh Acres, Port Charlotte, Palm Bay, Citrus Springs, Marion Oaks), plus a build-on-your-lot programme, which needs little land capital and is a poor fit for a classic land-bank structure. The opening for a land banker is the newer community business: it took finished homesites in West Port (111 lots, 2022) and Babcock Ranch (291 homes, 2023), and in September 2026 was named one of five builders in Barron Collier's 2,000-home Brightshore in Naples, alongside Pulte, Toll, Taylor Morrison and M/I. So it is a plausible but small land-banking customer, most likely for bulk finished-lot takedowns in master plans; how it funds those today is not public.

Credit ratings: None found (private; no public debt identified)
Metrics source: SJV Homes press release: No. 97 on the 2025 Builder 100 (552 closings and $245M revenue in 2024)
Land strategy: Owns through joint ventures rather than options: SJV Homes and Presidio Residential Capital close on land together (parcels sized for roughly 30 to 300 homes per community, per Presidio's Central Valley portfolio list, in Tulare, Kings, Kern and Fresno county towns) and develop and build it out in the venture. No stated owned/optioned target and no public mention of lot options or land banking. In February 2024 the company described a pipeline of nine new communities and expansions adding roughly 1,600 homes; in November 2026 it reported 19 active neighborhoods with four more scheduled (Keystone and Northgate in NW Visalia, Estrella and Mirabella in NW Hanford).
Financing summary: SJV Homes is a conventional private for-sale builder whose land and construction have been financed since 2013 through project joint ventures with one capital partner, Presidio Residential Capital of San Diego, which described itself in 2018 as funding 100 percent of SJV Homes' projects and operations and counted 40 joint communities and more than 5,000 homes by mid-2024. The joint venture buys land outright (raw or entitled parcels) and develops it; no land banker, lot-option provider, bank facility or note issue is publicly named for the builder itself, and nothing is filed publicly. Two things have changed in public view since 2024: Presidio has dropped out of the builder's press-release boilerplate (it still appeared in February 2024, not from February 2025 on), yet Presidio principal Paul Lucatuorto is listed as Co-CEO of SJV Homes on the October 2026 team page. Room for a land banker therefore depends on Presidio: it is either the incumbent to displace or, given its own committed capital was a stated $250M across 25-plus projects for all its builders, a partner that could use off-balance-sheet lot capital for a builder closing about 550 homes a year with four more neighborhoods coming from 2027.

Metrics source: HousingWire / The Builder's Daily: National Home Corp. targets 18% gross margin with pace focus
Land strategy: Land-light by design: buys finished lots from developers, builds standardized plans 100% spec, and aims to keep capital exposed for as short a time as possible (the Wade Jurney Homes playbook: just-in-time lot takedowns, fast inventory turns, pace over margin). No stated owned/optioned target. The company site runs a 'We Buy Lots' / 'Sell Land' page asking owners of developed homesites and build-for-rent partners to submit deals.
Financing summary: National Home Corp. is a private, founder-owned entry-level builder (550 closings in 2025, pacing 800+ in 2026) that buys finished lots only, builds 100% spec and describes its land exposure as limited; it does not develop land and publishes no lot count. A conventional for-sale builder that also sells to and fee-builds for build-to-rent investors, it is a plausible but small land-banking customer: its stated plan to reach about 1,200 homes under construction by year-end 2026 and 1,500 to 1,800 closings in 2027 implies a much larger finished-lot pipeline than it has needed so far, and its site openly solicits developed homesites from sellers. No land banker, lot-option financier, equity sponsor or credit facility is publicly named; the only lender names on record are from 2022 (Wells Fargo, 'Regents' as printed, Fifth Third and Flagstar funding start-up operations). The one disclosed joint venture is NHC Mortgage with loanDepot, a buyer-mortgage venture, not land capital. No public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found.

Land strategy: Not stated by the company. The site title calls it a 'Houston-based builder and developer', but the public pattern is buying finished lots section by section in third-party master-planned communities, plus smaller stand-alone subdivisions (for example Tidwell Lakes, where the site says a new section is coming in fall 2026, and the 50-home Regents Court infill community). Owned versus optioned split: not publicly disclosed.

What is visible is a finished-lot buyer: five of its 14 current communities (Sunterra, Lago Mar, Grand Magnolia, River Ranch, Cypress Green) are Land Tejas master plans where it builds alongside national builders, and the rest are smaller subdivisions and one 50-home infill site whose developers are not public. No land banker, lot-option financier or link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. Its one visible partnership is a mortgage joint venture, Colina Mortgage Group, LLC, co-owned with a Network Funding affiliate. It is a plausible but small land-banking customer (about 540 closings a year at entry-level prices), most likely for the stand-alone subdivisions it controls itself rather than for developer-supplied lots in master plans.

Land strategy: Mixed, with no stated owned-versus-optioned target. Delaware: lots come largely from the affiliated developer Ocean Atlantic Companies, which develops communities with investor equity and hands the home building to Schell Brothers. Richmond, Nashville, Boise: finished lots from third-party and master-plan developers, plus raw land put under contract and taken through rezoning by Schell's own division land directors. Pro Builder (Dec 2023) described large land holdings around Rehoboth Beach built up since the 2007-08 downturn.
Financing summary: Schell Brothers is a private, founder-controlled, conventional for-sale builder with no public debt, no ratings and no SEC filings found, so its bank lines and balance sheet are not public. What is public is the land model. In its Delaware home market, lots are largely developed by the Schell family's affiliated developer, Ocean Atlantic Companies (run by Chris Schell's twin brother Preston), which funds each project with outside investor equity alongside its own and has used institutional land capital before (a 2012 joint venture with Mountain Real Estate Capital). In Richmond, Nashville and Boise there is no affiliate: Schell buys lots that developers such as HHHunt build for it, contracts raw land subject to rezoning, and co-develops larger sites with another builder (Main Street Homes). No land banker, lot-option financier or link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon was found. It is a plausible land-banking customer, mainly for the three expansion divisions and for large self-assembled sites such as the 76-acre Westford Glen; in Delaware the affiliate and its investor base already fill that role, so the pitch there is to Ocean Atlantic as much as to Schell.

No land banker, lot-option financier or joint venture has been named publicly, and it has no public link to Domain, Millrose, Kennedy Lewis or TPG Angelo Gordon. It is a plausible but small land-banking prospect: about 530 closings a year, five new communities opened in 2026, and a stated aim to reach the top 50, all funded so far from an owned-land model.

Land strategy: Mostly owned and self-developed in the company's own framing ('land to warranty'): it acts as master developer at Everlee (Hoover, 800+ acres, about 2,300 planned homes, started 2022) and buys raw parcels itself (24 acres at Riverwalk Village, Hoover, January 2025). It has no public debt or SEC filings; HousingWire (Sept 2026) says it reports results to its lenders, but no lender, facility size or land-banking partner is named in public sources. Its ESOP held about $224.8M of employer stock at end-2024 against $44.2M of ESOP acquisition debt, so the company carries leverage tied to its ESOP. For a land banker it is a plausible but untested prospect: a profitable (H1 2026 net income $23.5M on $178.3M revenue), mostly presold builder with heavy owned-land and development exposure in Birmingham and new Nashville-area communities, and no public sign of lot-option or land-banking use.

Metrics source: Builder firm profile, Park Square Homes (archived 2026-07-21): closings 2025 522 / revenue $251M; 2024 996 / $311M; no balance-sheet data public
Land strategy: Mixed (no stated target): self-develops purchased land in its own communities and also buys finished lots from third-party developers; no owned/optioned split published.
Financing summary: Park Square Homes is a private, family-owned Florida builder (parent Park Square Enterprises, LLC) with no SEC filings, no rated or public debt and no published financial statements, so its bank lines and land financing are not public. Volume fell from 996 closings ($311M) in 2024 to 522 closings ($251M) in 2025 per Builder's 2026 firm profile, which is why it slipped from No. 70 to No. 100. It sources land both ways: it buys raw or partly entitled parcels and develops them itself (Sutton Lakes in Winter Garden, ~200 homes, groundbreaking planned 2026; 25 acres at Babcock Ranch for 242 townhomes, 2023; Phase 1 of Walton Global's Canopy master plan in Hernando County, 76.55 acres / up to 227 lots, 2024), and it takes finished lots under contract from developers (Keewin's Cypress Park Estates in Haines City, alongside D.R. Horton, Lennar and Dream Finders; Newland homesites for Tampa communities). No land banker, lot-option financier or outside equity partner is publicly linked to the homebuilder. The family's commercial arm Kimaya raises project equity from family offices, RIAs, fund managers and institutions for build-to-rent and multifamily, so the family is used to outside capital. For a land banker: a mid-size self-developing builder with falling volume (and a VP of Land opening seen only in search snippets) is a plausible lot-option customer, but the size of any facility is unknown.
